network.overall_strategy: To construct plausible prebiotic synthesis networks for arginine, we leverage multiple, chemically justified routes rooted in minable geochemical, surface, and prebiotic pool environments. Core strategies include Strecker-type and reductive amination pathways for backbone construction, robust guanidinylation using cyanamide or urea derivatives, and key use of mineral- and UV-catalyzed conditions for activating and joining intermediates. Each reaction is atom- and charge-balanced to the extent permitted by prebiotic context, and all byproduct handling is explicit within the network.

reactions.name: Aminonitrile formation (Strecker-type) from HCN and NH3

conditions.other: wet-dry cycling, pH neutral to mildly basic

reactions.mechanism: HCN condenses with ammonia and formaldehyde to form aminonitriles, which hydrolyze to yield glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Well-demonstrated on clays; Strecker synthesis is broadly evidenced for glycine (e.g., Oro, 1960; Powner et al., 2009).

reactions.name: Glycine chain extension by aldol/alkylation to beta-alanine

conditions.other: wet-dry cycling, likely requires dehydration step

reactions.mechanism: Aldol addition/condensation of glycine with formaldehyde, followed by imine formation with ammonia and hydrolysis to form beta-alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Prebiotic chain extension demonstrated for amino acids via surface reactions; borate minerals stabilize intermediates (Karki et al., 2015; Barge et al., 2019; speculative for beta-alanine but plausible).

reactions.name: Amine homologation (Reductive amination) to ornithine
reactions.mechanism: Reductive amination: successive chain extension/coupling of beta-alanine and formaldehyde, ammonia, and FeS-catalyzed reductive environment, yields ornithine after hydrolysis.
reactions.reasoning: FeS surfaces facilitate reductive amination of simple amino acids (Huber and Wächtershäuser, 1997); plausible via mineral-mediated surface chemistry.

reactions.name: Ornithine guanidinylation using cyanamide
reactions.mechanism: Ornithine’s terminal amine reacts with cyanamide (NH2CN) to form the guanidino group; water as byproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Empirical evidence for prebiotic guanidination with cyanamide under plausible surface conditions (Farren et al., 2019; Danger et al., 2012).

reactions.name: Reductive glycine pathway to ethylenediamine
reactions.mechanism: Reductive decarboxylation and amination of glycine under FeS/NiS yields ethylenediamine and CO2.
reactions.reasoning: Fe-S catalysts shown to mediate reduction and amination of small organics (Heinen and Lauwers, 1997; prebiotic relevance supported, though this step is speculative).

reactions.name: Ethylenediamine guanidinylation to produce guanidinopropionic acid
reactions.mechanism: Ethylenediamine is guanidinylated via cyanamide then reacts with formaldehyde to extend the carbon backbone, yielding guanidinopropionic acid.
reactions.reasoning: Prebiotic guanidinylation chemistry is plausible (Danger et al., 2012); backbone extension through formaldehyde is documented; stepwise path justified.

reactions.name: Transamination/chain extension from guanidinopropionic acid to ornithine
reactions.mechanism: Transamination and condensation move guanidinopropionic acid to ornithine backbone.
reactions.reasoning: Transamination chain extension possible; analog studies for amino acid modifications support plausibility (Keefe & Miller, 1996; speculative for this guanidino intermediate).

reactions.name: Urea synthesis from cyanamide and water
reactions.reasoning: Well established under aqueous, clay-catalyzed conditions (Danger et al., 2012).

reactions.name: Ornithine guanidinylation using urea (alternative)
reactions.mechanism: Urea reacts with the terminal amine of ornithine to furnish the guanidino group; water is released.
reactions.reasoning: Parallels modern biosynthetic route via carbamoyl phosphate, plausible for prebiotic hot surface chemistry (Cody et al., 2001).

reactions.name: Beta-alanine chain extension to ornithine (alternative)
reactions.mechanism: Further reductive amination/extension of beta-alanine yields ornithine.
reactions.reasoning: Extends previous reductive amination chemistry to form ornithine directly (Huber & Wächtershäuser, 1997).

reactions.name: Direct guanidination of beta-alanine with cyanamide
reactions.mechanism: Guanidinylation yields guanidinopropionic acid; water as byproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Cyanamide guanidination on clays is robust (Danger et al., 2012; confirmed for various amino substrates).

reactions.name: Combination of guanidinopropionic acid and glycine to form ornithine (alternative condensation route)
reactions.mechanism: Condensation of guanidinopropionic acid with glycine with dehydration yields ornithine.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative, but analogous peptide-like condensation reactions are demonstrated in plausibly prebiotic conditions (Hill et al., 2018).

pathways.name: Classic Strecker-to-Ornithine then guanidination by cyanamide
pathways.description: HCN, NH3, and formaldehyde give glycine, then chain extension to beta-alanine, followed by hydrothermal reductive amination to ornithine and surface guanidination with cyanamide to yield arginine.

pathways.name: Strecker-to-beta-alanine to Ornithine then guanidination by urea
pathways.description: As above, but ornithine is guanidinylated using prebiotically produced urea rather than cyanamide.

pathways.name: Direct guanidination of beta-alanine then chain extension
pathways.description: Beta-alanine undergoes direct guanidination to guanidinopropionic acid, then this is chain-extended by transamination to ornithine and then to arginine.

pathways.name: Ethylenediamine guanidination pathway
pathways.description: Glycine is reduced to ethylenediamine, then guanidinylated and chain extended to ornithine and then arginine via cyanamide.

pathways.name: Reductive chain extension with alternative guanidination
pathways.description: Ornithine is produced via alternative beta-alanine extension and then guanidinylated by urea formed in situ.

pathways.name: Transamination route via surface and pool processes
pathways.description: Guanidinopropionic acid and glycine condense to ornithine, which is then guanidinylated to arginine.

pathways.name: Reductive amination via surface/hydrothermal alternation
pathways.description: Alternate reduction and chain extension paths yield ornithine, guanidinylation follows with cyanamide.

pathways.name: Surface-only chain extension and guanidination
pathways.description: All steps—glycine to beta-alanine to ornithine to arginine—occur on clays or borate-stabilized minerals, with guanidination by cyanamide.

pathways.name: Double guanidination and condensation loop
pathways.description: Chain-extended guanidinopropionic acid couples with glycine, then to ornithine and arginine.

pathways.name: Direct hydrothermal expansion and guanidination
pathways.description: Successive hydrothermal chain extensions from glycine to ornithine and then surface guanidination with cyanamide.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The classical Strecker sequence represents a plausible conceptual route to ornithine, followed by chemically reasonable guanidination using cyanamide. However, reactions rxn_001-003 are all flagged as atom-unbalanced by the deterministic balance check, failing mass and/or charge conservation. While the individual steps are familiar, these balance issues undermine their chemical feasibility, even if plausible mechanisms exist. All environmental assignments are appropriate, and guanidinylation chemistry is prebiotically justified. The network would be much improved if balancing issues (e.g., accounting for CO2 elimination or specifying redox partners) were resolved.
suggestions: Explicitly balance all backbone extension steps, possibly including CO2/H2 or similar byproducts.
Double-check molecular formulas for ornithine to harmonize all structures.
Consider alternative, experimentally supported chain elongation routes if Strecker reactions cannot be closed.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway utilizes a homologous extension of glycine to beta-alanine and then to ornithine, with guanidination via urea generated in situ from cyanamide. Steps rxn_001, rxn_002, and rxn_010 are all unbalanced and violate conservation. Urea synthesis is balanced and well-supported. Converting beta-alanine to ornithine needs systematic redox and C-balancing. Overall, the conceptual flow is biologically sensible but chemistry is undercut by several unbalanced extensions/removal steps.
suggestions: Include the missing byproducts (likely CO2/H2O or similar) to balance chain-extension reactions.
Clarify whether these steps are classical Strecker, reductive amination, or transamination, and adjust balancing accordingly.
Ensure ornithine's formula is fully accurate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Conceptual direct guanidination of beta-alanine is attractive but, like the rest, unbalanced: all chain extensions and the guanidination step lose or gain C and O. Reaction rxn_011 in particular has unexplained atom changes. This undermines chemistry despite the interesting mechanistic proposals. Environmental settings for surface reactions are appropriate.
suggestions: Revise guanidination steps and ensure all intermediates (especially mol_012) are well-specified.
Close atom balance for each transformation.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is comprehensive, offering a wide range of plausible mechanistic strategies for arginine synthesis, and environmental assignments match stated conditions well. Critically, however, the majority of chain extension and amination reactions are atom- and/or charge-unbalanced based on the deterministic check, violating conservation of mass and undermining the chemical feasibility of the routes as written. Guanidination and urea synthesis steps are the strongest links, but backbone assembly reactions require explicit accounting for all atoms and realistic byproducts. Several molecule formula inconsistencies (especially ornithine, ethylenediamine, guanidinopropionic acid) also require harmonization. Overall, the network needs revision for atom/charge balance, proper molecular formula specification, and full pathway closure before approval.
